items.originalTitle: Nano Banana 2 Lite
items.summary:
DeepMind has released Nano Banana 2 Lite, also known as Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Image, which is designed as the fastest and most cost-effective Gemini image model optimized for speed and scalability. This model is accessible through their API and aims to deliver efficient image generation performance.

Simon Willison tested the model using AI Studio with a prompt to create a "Where's Waldo"-style image featuring a raccoon holding a ham radio. He noted that the results were improved compared to previous Nano Banana models, despite minor spelling errors in the generated image. The release highlights ongoing advancements in generative AI image models focused on balancing speed, cost, and quality.

items.summary:
Researchers have discovered that Claude AI embeds steganographic markers within user prompts, effectively encoding hidden information in the input data. This finding reveals that the AI system is not only processing user requests but also subtly tagging them in a way that may have implications for privacy and data tracking.

The analysis, detailed in a blog post on thereallo.dev, highlights how these embedded markers can be detected and decoded, raising questions about transparency and user consent in AI interactions. The discovery has sparked discussion about the ethical considerations of such practices in AI design and deployment.

items.title: Anthropic launches Claude Science, an AI-powered research platform for reproducible scientific analysis and manuscript drafting, available on macOS and Linux [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Science
items.summary:
Anthropic has launched Claude Science, a new AI-powered research platform designed to support reproducible scientific analysis and manuscript drafting. Available on macOS and Linux, the platform integrates data analysis, database searches, and scientific visualization tools, enabling researchers to trace every step from data processing to publication. Claude Science offers features such as built-in scientific renderers, persistent Python and R kernels, and automated fact-checking to enhance accuracy and reproducibility.

The platform is pre-configured for various life science domains including genomics, proteomics, and cheminformatics, and supports complex workflows like single-cell RNA-seq analysis and protein structure modeling. It manages computational resources across local machines and high-performance clusters, allowing scalable and efficient research. Users can draft manuscripts alongside their analyses, with all figures and data fully traceable to their source code, facilitating collaboration and review.

Claude Science aims to streamline scientific workflows by combining AI capabilities with domain-specific tools, helping researchers produce publication-quality results more efficiently. Early users have highlighted its transformative impact on non-computational biologists and its ability to uncover insights such as laboratory contaminants. The platform's extensibility and integration with existing lab tools position it as a comprehensive environment for modern scientific research.

items.title: Meta AI releases Brain2Qwerty v2, a non-invasive brain-to-text system decoding sentences in real time with up to 78% word accuracy, approaching surgical method performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From brain waves to words: a new path to communication without surgery
items.summary:
Meta AI has introduced Brain2Qwerty v2, an advanced non-invasive brain-to-text system that decodes sentences in real time with up to 78% word accuracy, nearing the performance of invasive surgical methods. This technology uses magnetoencephalography (MEG) to record brain activity and employs end-to-end deep learning combined with large language models to translate neural signals into coherent text.

The system was trained on data from nine volunteers who typed while wearing MEG devices, allowing the AI to learn from approximately 22,000 sentences. Brain2Qwerty v2 significantly outperforms previous non-invasive approaches, which had only about 8% word accuracy, and shows potential for further improvement through increased data volume.

Meta AI is releasing the full training code and datasets to encourage collaboration and accelerate neuroscience research. This development aims to provide scalable communication solutions for individuals with brain lesions who cannot communicate, offering a less invasive alternative to current neuroprosthetic methods.

These models aim to facilitate creative iteration and comprehensive multimedia experiences, allowing developers to build faster and more scalable generative media applications.

This employee liquidity event follows a similar tender offer conducted alongside Wayve's Series C funding in 2024, reflecting investor confidence in the company's growth prospects.

The proposal, which was developed with the assistance of artificial intelligence tools in collaboration with Stanford University's Regulation, Evaluation, and Governance Lab, raised concerns among supervisors and the board clerk about its broad scope and lack of clarity, making it difficult to understand the specific changes.

The ordinance sought to reduce outdated reporting requirements and streamline the code, which currently contains over 16 million words. However, supervisors noted that the legislative summary did not fully capture all changes, and some modifications, such as those related to gender pay tracking, warranted further scrutiny. The vote was postponed to allow more time for review and to ensure transparency and public understanding of the proposed legal revisions.

This analysis examines the impact of artificial intelligence on higher education by comparing it to previous technological disruptions such as the Internet, big data, and MOOCs. It explores whether AI will bring transformative changes or follow the pattern of past innovations that generated high expectations but resulted in limited fundamental shifts within educational institutions.

items.originalTitle: Serving Local AI on My Jetson Through Durable Streams
items.summary:
A developer has successfully deployed a local AI text-to-speech model on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, leveraging Durable Streams technology to enable reliable and shareable audio streaming. This setup allows users to submit text, select a voice, and receive a link to stream the generated speech incrementally, improving responsiveness and user experience compared to traditional request-response methods.

The Jetson Orin Nano, equipped with 1024 CUDA cores and 32 tensor cores, provides sufficient processing power for the Kokoro-82M neural text-to-speech model used in this project. Durable Streams facilitate a persistent, ordered sequence of audio chunks that can be accessed live or replayed later, ensuring robustness against network disruptions and enabling multiple users to access the audio without overloading the GPU.

This approach simplifies the architecture by avoiding complex infrastructure like queues or databases for job management, offering a clean API that supports various client interfaces. It demonstrates a practical reference design for local AI inference and streaming, highlighting the potential for edge computing applications that require efficient, low-latency AI services without relying on cloud providers.

items.title: Researchers present TraceRetain, a framework for selective memory retention in frozen LLM agents that improves task success and robustness under noisy conditions in ALFWorld benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Selective Memory Retention for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced TraceRetain, a framework designed to enhance memory retention in frozen large language model (LLM) agents by selectively managing external memory entries based on features like success, age, and relevance. Tested on the ALFWorld benchmark with the gpt-5-mini model, TraceRetain demonstrated improved task success and robustness, particularly under noisy conditions where traditional memory approaches degraded significantly. The framework maintains high precision by evicting less useful memory entries, effectively handling synthetic distractors and preserving task performance.

In controlled experiments, TraceRetain outperformed unbounded memory and FIFO retention policies, especially when 75% of memory writes were noisy distractors. While unbounded memory showed high similarity but low precision due to distractor interference, TraceRetain maintained stable precision and task success rates. Evaluations on held-out tasks confirmed that memory-augmented policies using TraceRetain solved more tasks than those without memory, highlighting its efficiency and robustness in long-horizon LLM agent applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When does retention matter for memory-augmented LLM agents? We study this with TraceRetain, a lightweight framework for bounded external memory in frozen LLM agents that scores entries by interpretable features (success, age, access frequency, redundancy, specificity, similarity, downstream utility) and evicts the lowest-scoring ones at capacity. On clean ALFWorld with gpt-5-mini, external memory robustly improves over no memory across two seeds, but differences among bounded retention policies fall within Wilson 95% CIs: clean ALFWorld at T=100 to T=200 does not naturally exhibit the memory pollution retention is designed to address. Under a controlled noisy-write stress (75% synthetic distractors), unbounded memory and FIFO-K50 degrade on Precision@5 (20.2% to 12.4% and 15.8% to 3.8%) while TraceRetain-CEM is essentially unchanged (16.9% to 16.6%) and preserves 97/100 task success. The mechanism: unbounded memory has the highest mean similarity (0.87) but lowest precision, indicating failed distractors close to the query in embedding space. Held-out in-distribution evaluation shows memory-augmented policies solving 47 to 49 of 50 tasks vs. 39/50 for no memory. Bounded retention buys memory and step efficiency on saturated clean benchmarks at no task-success cost, and only differentiates from cache heuristics when streams contain noise.

items.title: Researchers propose evidence-informed belief updates for large language models to improve continual scientific discovery by increasing non-stationary surprisal and reducing spurious rewards across five domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evidence-Informed LLM Beliefs for Continual Scientific Discovery
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method to improve continual scientific discovery using large language models (LLMs) by introducing evidence-informed belief updates. Unlike previous approaches that treated surprisal—a measure of how surprising new information is—as static, this method updates LLMs' prior beliefs with evidence from earlier hypotheses to calculate non-stationary surprisal, better reflecting how human reasoning evolves over time. This approach helps identify and reduce spurious rewards during hypothesis search, enhancing the discovery process.

The team compared various belief-updating mechanisms and found that embedding-based retrieval-augmented generation over prior discoveries most accurately predicted updated beliefs, revealing that over a third of static surprisals were misleading. They then modified the search procedure by incorporating belief-update filtering and diversity maximization to prioritize genuinely surprising hypotheses. Testing across five scientific domains showed a 30.62% average increase in accumulated non-stationary surprisal, demonstrating that effective continual discovery with LLMs requires both improved belief measurement and search strategies that avoid redundancy and promote diverse exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-ended scientific discovery with large language models (LLMs) increasingly operates as a long-horizon loop of hypothesis search and verification, where a reward signal guides which hypotheses to test next. A notable recent example is AutoDiscovery, which uses "Bayesian surprise" - the belief shift an LLM undergoes after observing evidence for a hypothesis - as both a discovery metric and a reward for search. We first observe that AutoDiscovery treats surprisal as a static quantity, while surprisal in human reasoning is non-stationary - it is defined relative to beliefs that evolve with experience, a prerequisite for continual scientific discovery. We address this mismatch with evidence-informed LLM beliefs: priors updated with evidence from previous hypotheses to compute non-stationary surprisal for new hypotheses. We compare in-context belief-updating mechanisms and find that embedding-based retrieval-augmented generation over prior discoveries best anticipates eventual posteriors, identifying 37.5% of static surprisals as spurious. We then modify search to avoid these spurious rewards and prioritize hypotheses that remain surprising under non-stationary beliefs. Concretely, we introduce two complementary changes to the original search procedure: belief-update filtering and diversity maximization. Across five discovery domains, our method increases accumulated non-stationary surprisal by 30.62% on average compared to the original search procedure, demonstrating that continual scientific discovery with LLMs requires not only better belief measurement but also search procedures that avoid redundancy and encourage diversity.

items.title: Researchers introduce EvalSafetyGap, a hybrid survey and conceptual framework analyzing LLM evaluation and safety failures across eight evidence streams from 2018 to 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EvalSafetyGap: A Hybrid Survey and Conceptual Framework for LLM Evaluation-Safety Failures
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced EvalSafetyGap, a hybrid survey and conceptual framework designed to analyze failures in large language model (LLM) evaluation and AI safety from 2018 to 2026. The framework combines systematic literature review, narrative synthesis, and a structured audit across eight evidence streams, including benchmark validity, safety evaluation, and governance. EvalSafetyGap uses Goodhart's Law and newly developed constructs to compare evaluation and alignment proxy failures under optimization pressure, aiming to clarify the relationship between capability, behavioral safety, and governance in LLMs.

The study's audit of ten models reveals that the correlation between model capability and sustained adversarial robustness is statistically inconclusive, with governance and disclosure playing a more significant role in the observed safety gaps than behavioral robustness. The findings highlight the variability introduced by different evaluation protocols and emphasize the need for dynamic evaluation, transparent reporting, and multi-attempt safety measurements. This work contributes a shared vocabulary and evidence map to support more auditable and reliable alignment practices in AI safety research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM evaluation and AI safety face a shared measurement problem: benchmark scores, reward-model signals, and reported safety metrics can improve while the latent properties they are meant to represent remain difficult to verify. This paper combines a hybrid survey - a systematic search paired with narrative synthesis and separately tracked grey evidence - with a conceptual framework and a structured ten-model audit. The synthesis spans eight evidence streams: benchmark validity, dynamic evaluation, LLM-as-judge reliability, safety evaluation, jailbreak/refusal robustness, reward hacking, mechanistic interpretability, and governance/auditability, covering 2018-2026 evaluation-safety measurement work. We introduce EvalSafetyGap as an organizing hypothesis for comparing evaluation-side and alignment-side proxy failures under optimization pressure, using Goodhart's Law together with two constructs we develop here - an Instability Decomposition and an Alignment Trilemma - as tools for generating testable comparisons. The audit shows how conclusions shift when capability, behavioral safety, and governance are measured separately. In this sample (n = 10), the association between capability and sustained adversarial robustness is statistically indeterminate using the displayed Table 3 inputs (Pearson r = +0.232, p = 0.520), and the apparent open-closed safety gap is modest, driven mainly by governance and disclosure rather than behavioral robustness, and sensitive to how a single borderline model is classified; attempt-budget results are protocol dependent. Because the public evidence uses heterogeneous protocols, the audit is diagnostic rather than rank-generating. The contribution is a shared vocabulary and evidence map to support dynamic evaluation, transparent source reporting, multi-attempt safety measurement, and auditable alignment practice.

items.title: Researchers introduce PixelRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation method using web page screenshots in pixel space that outperforms text-based baselines on Wikipedia and multimodal QA tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PIXELRAG: Web Screenshots Beat Text for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PixelRAG, a novel retrieval-augmented generation method that processes web pages as pixel-based screenshots rather than text. This approach preserves the visual layout and formatting of websites, allowing the system to perform retrieval and reading directly in pixel space without converting content to text. PixelRAG has been applied to a large-scale Wikipedia corpus, handling 30 million screenshot images with an efficient visual retrieval index, and it outperforms traditional text-based retrieval methods on various question-answering tasks.

Built on a visual embedding model fine-tuned with contrastive training on screenshot data, PixelRAG feeds retrieved images directly into a vision-language model. It shows significant improvements over text-based baselines on both text-centric and multimodal open-domain question-answering benchmarks, with accuracy gains up to 18.1%. Additionally, the pixel-based approach enables efficiency gains through image compression, reducing token costs by up to three times while maintaining accuracy.

These findings challenge the conventional reliance on text representations for web retrieval, suggesting that operating directly on the web's native visual form can enhance both performance and efficiency in retrieval-augmented generation systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28344v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Augmenting large language models (LLMs) with retrieved web text has become a dominant paradigm, yet the web is not natively textual: existing systems depend on complex parsing pipelines that linearize HTML and discard layout, visual structure, and formatting. We introduce PixelRAG, a new retrieval-augmented method that represents websites in their native visual form and performs retrieval and reading entirely in pixel space, enabling an end-to-end architecture that eliminates text abstraction. PixelRAG is, to our knowledge, the first pipeline to operate over a full Wikipedia corpus in this form, scaling to a datastore of 30 million screenshot images with an efficient visual retrieval index. Built on an existing visual embedding model (i.e., Qwen3-VL-Embedding), PixelRAG further fine-tunes this model on screenshot data with carefully curated contrastive training data. Retrieved screenshots are then fed directly as pixel inputs to a VLM, without intermediate text conversion. PixelRAG consistently outperforms both no-retrieval and text-based RAG baselines, most surprisingly on widely studied text-centric tasks such as NQ and SimpleQA. It also achieves strong gains on multimodal open-domain QA (e.g., MMSearch), benchmarks over noisy news corpora (e.g., LiveVQA), and agentic benchmarks (e.g., MoNaCo), improving accuracy by up to 18.1% over text-based baselines. Finally, pixel representations enable a new efficiency lever for RAG through image compression, achieving up to 3x token cost reduction at lower resolutions while maintaining accuracy. Our results challenge the necessity of text representations in web retrieval, suggesting that web RAG can operate directly in the web's native visual form while improving both performance and efficiency.

items.originalTitle: LoRA-Tuned Large Language Models for Dementia Detection via Multi-View Speech-Derived Features
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a low-rank adaptation (LoRA)-tuned large language model (LLM) that integrates multiple speech-derived features to detect dementia with high accuracy. By combining automatic speech recognition transcripts with pause markers, discourse-level topic cues, temporal fluency statistics, and phonological sequences into a unified prompt, the model achieves a 90.14% F1-score on the ADReSSo dataset without relying on separate modality-specific encoders or late-stage fusion.

This approach addresses limitations of previous methods that focused on single speech representations by enabling structured multi-view reasoning across diverse cognitive indicators reflected in spontaneous speech. Ablation studies confirm that each speech-derived feature contributes complementarily to the model's performance, highlighting the effectiveness of integrating heterogeneous speech signals for early dementia detection.

On ADReSSo, our best model achieves an F1-score of 90.14%, and ablation confirms the complementary contribution of each view.

items.title: Researchers propose SCSuff metric to evaluate sufficiency of large language model explanations based on models' own input beliefs, finding explanations generally insufficient and varying with input distribution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What LLMs explain is not what they believe: Evaluating explanation sufficiency under models' own input beliefs
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new metric called SCSuff to evaluate the sufficiency of free-text explanations provided by large language models (LLMs). This metric assesses whether explanations contain enough information to accurately reflect the model's output-generating process by using the model itself to generate alternative inputs based on the explanation, capturing its internal beliefs. Their findings reveal that explanations from LLMs are generally insufficient and that sufficiency varies depending on the input distribution.

The study extends classical sufficiency concepts to arbitrary explanations and demonstrates that explanation sufficiency depends on the defined input distribution. Experiments show that SCSuff aligns with targeted perturbation tests and that explanation quality is only weakly related to model size, accuracy, or output entropy. Analysis of internal model states suggests that SCSuff can help identify and improve explanation sufficiency, offering a new tool for evaluating and enhancing LLM interpretability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains, where free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought and post-hoc rationales are used to justify model outputs. We find LLM explanations are generally insufficient and weakly correlated with model size, accuracy, or output entropy. Analysis of final-token hidden states shows that top and bottom SCSuff scores can be predicted from internal representations, suggesting that SCSuff can guide detection and improvement of sufficient LLM explanations. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/rajesh-lab/self-consistent-sufficiency .

items.title: Researchers find that excessive test-time sampling in language models can worsen answer selection due to a modal ceiling and correlation ceiling limiting effective sample use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When More Sampling Hurts: The Modal Ceiling and Correlation Ceiling of Test-Time Scaling
items.summary:
Researchers have found that excessive test-time sampling in language models, a technique used to improve reasoning by generating multiple answers, can actually degrade performance when selecting the final answer. While increasing the number of samples raises the chance of producing a correct response somewhere among them, the process of choosing the best answer is limited by what the model can confidently identify, leading to a plateau known as the modal ceiling. Beyond this point, additional samples increase computational cost without improving—and sometimes worsening—the final selection.

The study introduces the concept of an "effective number of samples," a metric that captures the optimal cutoff for sampling during test-time scaling. It highlights that the main challenge lies not in generating correct answers but in recognizing and selecting them accurately. This finding suggests that language models should limit their sampling efforts to a moderate number to balance accuracy and efficiency, as excessive sampling offers diminishing returns and may reinforce confident mistakes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People overthink; language models over-sample, and the extra effort can talk both into a worse answer. Reasoning systems answer a hard question by sampling it many times (test-time scaling), and the more they draw, the more often a correct answer turns up somewhere, so coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct try, climbs and appears to be progress. But a deployed system must return one answer, and choosing it, not knowing which try is right, is selection; selection is capped, and past a point extra samples only make the model surer of a confident mistake, even as every draw adds cost. The gap between climbing coverage and stalled selection, the identifiability gap, is the answer a model can produce but not pick. So the real question is not whether to sample but how far, and the answer is: not far. For picking an answer, the vote has already settled within a few dozen draws, the modal ceiling; for scoring a benchmark, sooner still, the correlation ceiling. Beyond that, extra draws cost compute and add nothing, and can even make the answer worse. This paper turns the cutoff into a single number, the effective number of samples, that any sampling run already reveals. The bottleneck is recognizing a right answer, not generating one.

items.title: Researchers find clinical evidence strength is encoded in language model representations but not reflected in their stated confidence grades across multiple frameworks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The strength of clinical evidence is recoverable from language model representations but not from their stated grades
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed 22 large language models (LLMs) to determine if these models encode the strength of clinical evidence in their internal representations and whether they explicitly convey this information. Using a dataset of over 45,000 clinical claims graded under multiple evidence frameworks, they found that while a linear estimator could recover evidence strength from the models' activations with moderate accuracy, the models' own stated confidence grades were no better than chance. This indicates that LLMs internally represent evidence strength but fail to communicate it effectively in their outputs.

The study revealed that the recoverable signal was largely lexical and did not generalize well across different topics or grading frameworks, yet it remained distinct from factual truth and could still identify weakly supported claims. Notably, larger model size did not improve the decodability of evidence strength, and reasoning-focused models showed the weakest signal. These findings suggest that clinical LLMs possess latent information about evidence support that is not reflected in their expressed confidence, highlighting a gap between internal representation and external communication in AI-assisted clinical summarization.

Yet these models convey confidence poorly, and properties they never state, such as truth, are often readable from their activations. Whether a clinical model registers evidence strength, distinct from truth, and states it when asked is untested, and any such signal could be lexical. We compiled 45,134 clinical claims from six public sources, harmonized 20,611 into a four-level evidence grade under three independent frameworks, and tested 22 local, open-weight LLMs from several developers (0.6-70 billion parameters; general, medical, and reasoning), with lexical, truth, and cross-framework controls. A linear estimator recovered the grade in every model (median AUROC 71.8), yet decodability did not rise with scale and was weakest in reasoning models. The grade the models stated fell to chance, 25-27 percentage points below the estimator. The recoverable signal was largely lexical and did not transfer across topics or frameworks, yet it was distinct from factual truth and still flagged weakly supported claims (AUROC 69.2). Clinical LLMs thus carry an ordered evidence-strength signal they do not express, so their stated grades fail to convey a claim's support even when it is recoverable from their representations and text.

items.title: Researchers introduce Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution to trace training data influence on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct's behavioral policies, revealing safety gaps and feature interference in 200 fine-tuning pairs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing Training Influence to Learned Behavioral Policies
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution (SMDA), a new framework that links specific training data pairs to the symbolic policies guiding a model's behavior. Applying SMDA to Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, they analyzed 200 supervised fine-tuning pairs to trace how training examples influence refusal behavior, revealing safety gaps and feature interference in the model's learned policies.

SMDA uses Ridge regression over sparse autoencoder features to model target behaviors and decomposes the impact of each training example through changes in feature activation and output probabilities. This approach exposes systematic weaknesses in the base model's safety responses, explains differing influences of harmful versus harmless training pairs, and identifies cases where training data affects unintended features.

By combining mechanistic interpretability with data attribution, SMDA offers a more detailed and scalable diagnostic tool than traditional black-box influence methods or manual circuit analysis, enhancing understanding of how training data shapes high-level model behaviors.

items.originalTitle: Deterministic Decisions for High-Stakes AI. A Zero-Egress Pipeline with the Deployability of RAG and the Accuracy of Machine Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a previously unquantified issue called intervention bias in zero-shot large language model (LLM) educational advisors, where these models recommend unnecessary actions despite an oracle policy indicating inaction is optimal. Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, they found that zero-shot GPT-4o recommended interventions for 73% of students at day 56, while the oracle suggested only 29% needed intervention, resulting in a 43 percentage-point false-positive rate. Similar miscalibration was observed in commercial retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and SQL-augmented retrieval systems. The study demonstrates that supervised policy learning methods, including a trajectory-conditioned Decision Transformer and an XGBoost classifier trained on oracle-labeled data, effectively eliminate this bias and achieve near-zero calibration error with high accuracy and low latency.

The research validates decision-making under controlled oracle input from structured data, emphasizing that the key finding is the contrast in intervention bias rather than absolute accuracy metrics. Additionally, the study highlights an evaluation gap where LLM-based scoring methods fail to detect intervention bias, often favoring fluent but excessive recommendations over decision quality. These insights suggest that supervised learning approaches can improve the reliability of AI-driven educational advisory systems by reducing unnecessary interventions.

items.originalTitle: Closing the Activation-Cone Blind Spot: Response-Time Probing and Unified Defense
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a systematic evaluation of five defense methods against five types of attacks on seven instruction-tuned large language models ranging from 7 to 31 billion parameters. They found that prompt-time activation defenses are inherently ineffective against prefilling attacks, with AlphaSteer showing zero success against most attacks but only 50% effectiveness on prefilling. To address this, they introduced response-time probing, a technique using a linear probe on the model's hidden states during initial token generation, achieving near-perfect accuracy in detecting prefilling attacks and reducing their success to zero without false positives.

The study demonstrated that combining response-time probing with AlphaSteer's null-space steering creates a complementary defense system that effectively counters both prefilling and semantic attacks, achieving high defense success rates on models like Mistral and Llama. Additionally, the researchers highlighted limitations in existing evaluation metrics and showed that diverse negative training data significantly reduces false positives in probing. They have released their code, attack methods, and detailed results to support further research in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29441v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Inference-time safety methods for large language models have proliferated, yet no systematic comparison exists. We evaluate five defense paradigms (no defense, static steering, CAST, AlphaSteer, probe-gated) across seven instruction-tuned models (7-31B) and five attack types (GCG, AutoDAN, DeepInception, prefilling, intent laundering). Our central finding: prompt-time activation defenses are structurally blind to prefilling attacks. AlphaSteer achieves 0% attack success on GCG, AutoDAN, and intent laundering but 50% on prefilling. We prove a corollary: any defense that gates intervention on a single layer's activation alignment with a benign reference (cone, subspace, or null-space) is blind to attacks that craft activations to lie inside that reference, whether checked at prompt time or per token. As its constructive contrapositive we introduce response-time probing: a linear probe on the model's hidden state at the first generated tokens, with AUROC 0.97-1.00 across all seven models. Combined with a halt, it cuts prefilling attack success to 0/40 on every model with 0% benign false positives, outperforming Llama Guard 3. Cross-template generalisation depends on probe depth, so we scope the claim to the canonical prefilling-template family. Composing the response-halt with AlphaSteer's null-space steering gives an orthogonal split (the halt catches prefilling, AlphaSteer catches semantic attacks), reaching defense success 0.983 on Mistral and 0.994 on Llama and dominating both components. We further show MMLU fails to capture steering's true utility cost, which appears as behavioral hedging rather than factual loss, and that diverse negative training sets cut probe false positives from 80-100% to near zero. Code, attacks, per-sample results, and the judge prompt are released.

items.summary:

The system autonomously generates and tests design hypotheses related to metal nodes, linkers, pore geometry, and functional chemistry, refining its approach over multiple iterations. It efficiently identifies top-performing MOFs across various tasks, including adsorption, separation, and electronic structure, without prior knowledge of the global property landscape.

LLM4MOF operates by having one agent propose design hypotheses and another translate these into constraints to select candidate MOFs, which are then evaluated through diagnostic tests to determine the influence of different design factors. The framework also generates new MOFs de novo and validates them through live simulations, adapting geometries to specific conditions. It outperforms random search and genetic algorithms in efficiency and cost, demonstrating that language-model agents can conduct interpretable, simulation-based inverse design without needing to train separate models for each objective.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inverse design of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) requires searching a combinatorially vast space where property labels are expensive and most machine-learning models reveal little about why a structure succeeds. We introduce LLM4MOF, a closed-loop framework in which language-model agents reason about chemistry, build candidate MOFs, and test them in simulation, refining hypotheses over ten autonomous iterations. One agent proposes interpretable design hypotheses over metal nodes, linkers, pore geometry, and functional chemistry, and a second translates them into constraints that select candidate MOFs, each made of a metal node, organic linker, and matching topology. Each hypothesis is tested through four diagnostic beams that apply different subsets of its constraints, so comparing them shows whether geometry, chemistry, or metal choice drives performance. Even when blind to the global property landscape of databases, LLM4MOF concentrates its search on top-performing structures across six adsorption, separation, and electronic-structure tasks within 400 property evaluations. The same loop also generates new MOFs de novo and validates them in live simulation, where it adapts the geometry to each requested condition, outperforming random search and a genetic algorithm at roughly $1 per campaign. LLM4MOF shows that language-model agents can run interpretable, simulation-grounded inverse design without training a model per objective.

items.originalTitle: Hybrid Retriever Evolution for Multimodal Document Reasoning Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a failure-driven evolution framework that enables a meta-agent to autonomously coordinate diverse retrievers—lexical, semantic, and multimodal—during multi-step multimodal document question answering. This approach transforms retrieval from a fixed initial step into an adaptive, step-wise reasoning process, allowing the agent to learn when and how to invoke different retrievers and combine evidence across modalities and pages. The evolved agent demonstrated significant performance improvements, achieving up to 19.6-point gains on benchmarks like MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench, outperforming recent systems such as MACT, MDocAgent, and SimpleDoc.

The framework works by analyzing incorrect reasoning trajectories and iteratively rewriting the task agent's instructions to improve retrieval coordination. Detailed analyses show that the gains result from adaptive routing and evidence composition rather than reliance on any fixed retrieval mode. The evolution process reveals a shift from narrow lexical retrieval to rich multi-tool coordination, highlighting the potential of autonomous multi-agent coordination as a promising paradigm for multimodal document reasoning.

The evolved agent learns when to invoke each retriever, how to combine them, and how to compose evidence across modalities and pages. On MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench, the evolved agent achieves gains of up to +19.6 points over the unevolved baseline and consistently outperforms recent systems including MACT, MDocAgent, and SimpleDoc. Detailed retrieval analyses confirm that these improvements arise from adaptive routing and evidence composition rather than reliance on any hard coded retrieval mode, and evolution dynamics reveal a progressive shift from narrow lexical behavior to rich multi-tool coordination. These findings establish autonomous multi-agent coordination as a promising paradigm for multimodal document reasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29706v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Telecom question answering (QA) is a challenging setting for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): evidence is fragmented across standards, papers, encyclopedic resources, and web documents, and answers often hinge on technical tables, equations, and specialized protocol language. In low-resource subdomains, generator fine-tuning can over-specialize and degrade general capability, making query-side retriever adaptation an attractive alternative. To this end, we ask whether a fixed-generator, query-adapted RAG system can outperform generator-side adaptation, and which retriever objectives best support that setting. We motivate retrieval, rather than generator fine-tuning, as the adaptation target through a capacity comparison: under bounded-parameter and soft-retrieval assumptions, query-encoder tuning can have a smaller estimation term than supervised fine-tuning when its effective dimension is smaller. We identify two particularly relevant objectives -- the latent-document RAG likelihood, which optimizes generation utility, and the InfoNCE contrastive objective, which improves semantic retrieval geometry -- and leverage them jointly through a retriever optimization method targeting downstream QA performance in the telecom domain. Specifically, we introduce ARMOR, Adaptive Regularized Mixture Optimization for Retrievers, which learns separate temperatures for the RAG retrieval distribution and InfoNCE softmax and regularizes the adapted query encoder toward the frozen base query encoder. Across telecom-specific retrieval and generative QA benchmarks, we show that ARMOR improves evidence retrieval and answer generation in several in-domain settings. Code is available at https://github.com/heshandevaka/ARMOR.git.

items.summary:

This work highlights the importance of aligning reward granularity with output complexity in reinforcement learning tasks involving multi-component generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucination is the reliability bottleneck for LLM-based agents, and fact attribution verifiers are the last line of defense -- yet today's verifiers emit only opaque binary labels, leaving agents unable to self-correct and operators unable to audit. We present SEVA, a structured verification agent that emits evidence alignments, step-by-step reasoning chains, calibrated confidence, and a six-category error diagnosis with actionable fixes. Training such an agent with RL is non-trivial: standard binary reward on multi-component output triggers advantage collapse -- within-group reward variance vanishes and the GRPO gradient disappears. We resolve this with a process reward that decomposes verification quality into five independent components weighted 70/30 toward process signals, restoring the gradient and inducing an implicit curriculum -- the agent first masters verification behavior (alignment 0.917 -> 0.997, format 72% -> 100%), then outcomes (F1 64.9 -> 69.0). Structured output further enables a Verify -> Reflect -> Probe -> Refine self-evolution loop, which over four rounds on a 7B model surfaces an unexpected structural finding: each round produces a benchmark-specialist, not a generalist (+15 pp on HaluEval, -10 to -14 pp on TruthfulQA in the same model, persistent at 4x data). On ClearFacts, SEVA-3B matches GPT-4o-mini (69.0 vs. 69.8 F1) while producing substantially richer, auditable output -- confirming a principle that should generalize: for any RL task with multi-component generation, reward granularity must match output granularity.

items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MATCH, a new framework designed to enhance the efficiency and scalability of large language models by improving sparse attention mechanisms in long-context transformers. MATCH integrates dynamic in-context retrieval through an efficient retrieval system, addressing the limitations of traditional attention methods that suffer from high computational costs and performance drops in long-range tasks. MATCH overcomes the common trade-off between efficiency and accuracy found in existing methods that rely on fixed local attention windows, which often degrade performance on tasks requiring precise long-range recall. By dynamically incorporating relevant contextual information, MATCH maintains the computational benefits of sparse attention while enhancing the model's ability to retrieve and utilize important information from extended contexts.

The development of MATCH highlights its potential as a versatile solution for improving in-context retrieval capabilities in large language models, paving the way for more effective and scalable applications in natural language processing tasks that involve long sequences.

items.originalTitle: SABER-Math: Automated Benchmark for Information Retrieval Evaluation in Mathematics
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SABER-Math, the first fully automated benchmark designed to evaluate mathematical information retrieval (IR) systems without requiring expert annotations. Utilizing a dataset of 283,000 high-school math problems and solutions, SABER-Math creates reranking tasks by extracting solution summaries and topics with large language models (LLMs), identifying relevant documents through topic and lexical similarities, and generating fine-grained relevance ratings via an LLM-based preference tournament. This benchmark addresses the challenge of assessing IR systems' effectiveness in mathematical contexts, where traditional benchmarks often fail to capture nuanced relevance.

The study evaluated various retrieval methods, including lexical retrievers, specialized mathematical systems, and modern embedding models. Results showed that while embedding models outperform classical and math-specific baselines, they still face difficulties in symbol-intensive areas like Algebra and Calculus. Additionally, the research highlights that general-purpose IR benchmarks, such as MTEB, do not reliably predict performance in mathematical retrieval tasks, underscoring the importance of domain-specific evaluation tools like SABER-Math.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.29894v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As agentic AI systems tackle more complex mathematical tasks, they increasingly rely on information retrieval (IR) to search problem databases, theorem libraries, and educational resources. However, choosing the right retriever remains difficult, as it is infeasible to directly isolate its effect on downstream performance. On the other hand, existing retrieval-specific benchmarks often fail to capture fine-grained mathematical relevance, penalizing relevant documents. We address this gap by introducing SABER-Math, the first fully automated benchmark for evaluating mathematical IR without expert annotation. Starting from 283K high-school-level math problems with solutions, SABER-Math builds challenging reranking tasks in three steps: (i) first, LLMs extract concise solution summaries and mathematical topics for each problem; (ii) then, per-query relevant documents are discovered using ontology topic-based and lexical solutions-summary-based similarities, and (iii) finally, a Swiss-style LLM preference tournament produces fine-grained relevance ratings for the documents. We evaluate lexical retrievers, specialized mathematical retrieval systems, and recent embedding models. We find that while modern embedding models substantially outperform classical and math-specific baselines, even the strongest systems struggle in symbol-heavy domains like Algebra and Calculus. Importantly, we show that general-purpose IR benchmarks such as MTEB do not reliably predict mathematical performance, especially for recent embedding models, highlighting the need for math-specific retrieval benchmarks.

items.originalTitle: Field Order Should Not Matter: Permutation-Invariant Embedding Model Fine-Tuning for Structured Metadata Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that the order of fields in structured metadata records significantly affects retrieval quality when using fine-tuned text encoders. They propose a permutation-invariant fine-tuning method (PI-FT) that randomizes field order and applies random field dropout during training, ensuring the model binds meaning to field labels rather than their positions. This approach reduces the retrieval performance drop caused by changes in field order from 7.4 to 0.2 nDCG@10 points with minimal impact on accuracy.

The study focuses on a catalog of nearly 10,000 development statistics indicators searchable across 15 languages using a 118M-parameter encoder suitable for self-hosting. To address the lack of training data for rarely searched indicators, the team generated queries using large language models, creating the DevDataBench benchmark. The fine-tuned encoder outperformed all zero-shot baselines, especially in low-resource languages. The researchers have released the benchmark, models, and PI-FT framework to support further development in structured metadata retrieval.

Embedding a record with a text encoder first serializes its fields into a string, which forces a choice of field order. We show this choice, usually treated as an implementation detail, silently controls retrieval quality once the encoder is fine-tuned. items.title: Researchers propose distributionally robust reinforcement learning from human feedback to improve large language model fine-tuning and out-of-distribution task performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Distributionally Robust Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a distributionally robust reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) approach to enhance the fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) and improve their performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. This method addresses the limitations of existing RLHF techniques, which often degrade when the downstream task differs significantly from the training data. The team formulated distributionally robust optimization versions of two fine-tuning methods—reward-based RLHF and reward-free direct preference optimization (DPO)—and proposed minibatch gradient descent algorithms with proven convergence guarantees.

The researchers evaluated their approach by training models on the Unified-Feedback dataset and testing them on different datasets to simulate OOD scenarios. Results demonstrated that the robust training improved the accuracy of learned reward models overall, with notable gains in tasks such as reasoning. Additionally, the robust policy optimization methods showed enhanced performance on OOD tasks, suggesting that this approach can help maintain model effectiveness when facing diverse or shifted input distributions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2503.00539v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has evolved to be one of the main methods for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). However, existing RLHF methods are non-robust, and their performance deteriorates if the downstream task differs significantly from the preference dataset used in fine-tuning. In order to mitigate this problem, we introduce a distributionally robust RLHF for fine-tuning LLMs. In particular, our goal is to ensure that a fine-tuned model retains its performance even when the distribution of prompts significantly differs from the distribution encountered during fine-tuning. We formulate distributionally robust optimization (DRO) version of two popular fine-tuning methods -- (1) reward-based RLHF and (2) reward-free DPO (direct preference optimization). We propose a minibatch gradient descent based algorithms for both of them, and theoretically prove convergence guarantees for the algorithms. Subsequently, we evaluate our algorithms on an out-of-distribution (OOD) task by first training the model on the Unified-Feedback dataset and evaluating its performance on two different datasets. The experimental results show that our robust training improves the accuracy of the learned reward models on average, and markedly on some tasks, such as reasoning. Furthermore, we show that the robust versions of policy optimization methods, similarly improve performance on OOD tasks.

items.title: Researchers develop post-training method to improve large language models' convention formation and communication efficiency, validated on two new benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Post-training for Efficient Communication via Convention Formation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a post-training method to enhance large language models' ability to form communication conventions and improve efficiency in multi-turn interactions. This approach involves targeted fine-tuning on selected examples of convention formation, addressing a limitation where prior models did not naturally exhibit this adaptive behavior. The method was validated using two new benchmarks: a cognitively motivated interaction task that elicits strong convention formation in humans, and a document-grounded reference completion task reflecting real-world communication patterns.

The study demonstrates that large language models subjected to this post-training process show significant improvements in developing and using ad-hoc conventions during communication. These findings suggest that fine-tuning on specific interaction patterns can help models better mimic human-like adaptive communication, potentially enhancing their performance in complex conversational settings.

items.title: Researchers train small attention-only transformers achieving perfect indirect object identification with minimal circuits specialized into additive and contrastive subcircuits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Emergence of Minimal Circuits for Indirect Object Identification in Attention-Only Transformers
items.summary:
Researchers have trained small, attention-only transformer models from scratch to perform the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task, a benchmark for coreference-like reasoning. Remarkably, a single-layer transformer with just two attention heads achieved perfect accuracy without using multilayer perceptrons or normalization layers. Analysis revealed that these two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that work together to resolve IOI, demonstrating that minimal, interpretable circuits can emerge from task-specific training.

Further investigation showed that a two-layer, one-head model primarily composes information through query-key interactions from the previous layer. These findings provide a controlled environment for studying the computational mechanisms underlying transformer reasoning and highlight the potential for mechanistic interpretability in understanding language models.

items.title: Researchers introduce Value-Action Alignment Rate to assess privacy and prosocial value conflicts in large language models' data-sharing decisions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Value-Action Alignment in Large Language Models under Privacy-Prosocial Conflict
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new method called the Value-Action Alignment Rate (VAAR) to evaluate how large language models (LLMs) balance privacy concerns and prosocial motivations when making decisions about personal data sharing. This approach uses a context-based protocol that sequentially measures privacy attitudes, prosocialness, and willingness to share data within a single session, allowing for a more integrated assessment of how these values influence the models' actions.

The study employs multi-group structural equation modeling to analyze the relationships between privacy concerns, prosocial behavior, and data-sharing decisions across different LLMs. Findings reveal that while each model exhibits stable but distinct profiles regarding privacy and prosocial attitudes, there is significant variation in how well their expressed values align with their actual data-sharing behaviors, highlighting heterogeneity in value-action consistency among these models.

We introduce a context-based assessment protocol that sequentially administers standardized questionnaires for privacy attitudes, prosocialness, and acceptance of data sharing within a bounded, history-carrying session. Across multiple LLMs, we observe stable but model-specific Privacy-PSA-AoDS profiles, and substantial heterogeneity in value-action alignment.

items.originalTitle: Lost in Execution: On the Multilingual Robustness of Tool Calling in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MLCL, a diagnostic benchmark designed to evaluate the robustness of multilingual tool calling in large language models (LLMs). Their study focuses on three languages—Chinese, Hindi, and the low-resource language Igbo—and reveals that while LLMs often understand user intent and select the correct tools, they frequently fail due to parameter value language mismatches. This occurs when models generate parameter values in the user's language, which conflicts with language-invariant execution requirements.

The research includes a detailed error analysis and tests several inference-time strategies to mitigate these language-induced execution errors. Although these strategies improve performance, none fully restore the models to the level of accuracy seen in English-centric evaluations, highlighting ongoing challenges in multilingual tool integration for LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.05366v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that invoke external tools through structured function calls. While recent work reports strong tool-calling performance under standard English-centric evaluations, the robustness of tool calling under multilingual user interactions remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce MLCL, a diagnostic benchmark, and conduct a systematic evaluation of multilingual tool calling across Chinese, Hindi, and the low-resource language Igbo. Through fine-grained error analysis, we show that many failures occur despite correct intent understanding and tool selection. We identify parameter value language mismatch as a dominant failure mode, where models generate semantically appropriate parameter values in the user's language, violating language-invariant execution conventions. We further evaluate several inference-time system strategies and find that while these strategies substantially reduce language-induced execution errors, none of them can fully recover English-level performance.

items.title: Researchers propose a longitudinal NLP modeling and evaluation paradigm for behavioral sequences, updating pipeline components and demonstrating improved accuracy on 17k diary transcripts with PTSD data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Word Sequences to Behavioral Sequences: Adapting Modeling and Evaluation Paradigms for Longitudinal NLP
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a new longitudinal modeling and evaluation framework for natural language processing (NLP) that addresses the limitations of treating documents as independent and unordered samples. This approach updates four key components of the NLP pipeline to better handle person-indexed, time-ordered behavioral sequences, including evaluation splits aligned with generalization over individuals and time, accuracy metrics distinguishing between-person differences from within-person dynamics, sequence inputs that incorporate history, and model structures supporting varying levels of latent state detail. The framework was tested on a dataset of 17,000 daily diary transcripts linked to PTSD symptom severity from 238 participants, revealing that traditional document-level evaluations can produce substantially different and sometimes opposite conclusions compared to this more ecologically valid method.

The study highlights the importance of shifting from conventional word-sequence evaluation toward behavior-sequence paradigms in NLP, especially for longitudinal data where temporal and individual context are critical. By incorporating history and distinguishing between different sources of variation, the proposed paradigm offers improved accuracy and more meaningful insights into behavioral patterns over time.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.07988v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While NLP typically treats documents as independent and unordered samples, in longitudinal studies, this assumption rarely holds: documents are nested within authors and ordered in time, forming person-indexed, time-ordered $\textit{behavioral sequences}$. Here, we demonstrate the need for and propose a longitudinal modeling and evaluation paradigm that consequently updates four parts of the NLP pipeline: (1) evaluation splits aligned to generalization over people ($\textit{cross-sectional}$) and/or time ($\textit{prospective}$); (2) accuracy metrics separating between-person differences from within-person dynamics; (3) sequence inputs to incorporate history by default; and (4) model internals that support different $\textit{coarseness}$ of latent state over histories (pooled summaries, explicit dynamics, or interaction-based models). We demonstrate the issues ensued by traditional pipeline and our proposed improvements on a dataset of 17k daily diary transcripts paired with PTSD symptom severity from 238 participants, finding that traditional document-level evaluation can yield substantially different and sometimes reversed conclusions compared to our ecologically valid modeling and evaluation. We tie our results to a broader discussion motivating a shift from word-sequence evaluation toward $\textit{behavior-sequence}$ paradigms for NLP.

items.title: Researchers introduce test-time detoxification method for large language models using zeroth-order optimization without retraining or learning auxiliary components [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Test-Time Detoxification without Training or Learning Anything
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a test-time detoxification method for large language models that reduces toxic or inappropriate text generation without requiring retraining or additional learned components. This approach uses zeroth-order optimization to approximate the gradient of toxicity with respect to input embeddings and applies a few descent steps to guide the model toward safer outputs. It only needs access to input embeddings, a toxicity scoring function, and forward model evaluations, making it applicable even in black-box settings.

The method has been shown to effectively lower toxicity across various models and prompts while maintaining high generation quality. By treating word embeddings as control variables, this technique offers a scalable and training-free way to enhance the safety of autoregressive language models, encouraging broader use of black-box optimization for safer text generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.02498v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models can produce toxic or inappropriate text even for benign inputs, creating risks when deployed at scale. Detoxification is therefore important for safety and user trust, particularly when we want to reduce harmful content without sacrificing the model's generation quality. Many existing approaches rely on model retraining, gradients, or learned auxiliary components, which can be costly and may not transfer across model families or to truly black-box settings. We introduce a test-time procedure that approximates the gradient of completion toxicity with respect to the input embeddings and uses a small number of descent steps to steer generation toward less toxic continuations. This is achieved with zeroth-order optimization that requires only access to input embeddings, a toxicity scoring function, and forward evaluations of the model. Empirically, the approach delivers robust toxicity reductions across models and prompts and, in most settings, achieves the best overall toxicity-quality trade-off. More broadly, our work positions word embeddings as effective control variables and encourages wider use of black-box optimization to guide autoregressive language models toward scalable, safer text generation, without requiring any training or access to intermediate computations.

items.title: Researchers propose Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding to improve structured generation accuracy in large language models by up to 24 percentage points without additional training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Hidden Cost of Structured Generation in LLMs: Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding (DCCD), a novel two-step, training-free method designed to improve the accuracy of structured generation in large language models (LLMs). This approach first generates an unconstrained draft and then applies constrained decoding conditioned on this draft to ensure syntactic validity, addressing issues where traditional constrained decoding can lead to semantically incorrect outputs despite valid syntax. DCCD has demonstrated improvements in strict structured accuracy by up to 24 percentage points on benchmarks such as GSM8K, significantly enhancing performance without additional training.

The method works by separating semantic planning from structural enforcement, which increases the feasible output space and reduces the negative effects of hard constraints during decoding. This allows smaller models to achieve or surpass the performance of larger constrained models, offering substantial gains in parameter efficiency. The researchers analyzed DCCD through a KL-projection framework and also introduced an optional best-of-K draft selection to further boost results.

These advancements suggest that DCCD can make structured output generation more reliable and efficient in practical applications involving executable code, JSON, and API calls, where syntax errors can render outputs unusable. By improving both accuracy and efficiency, this technique has the potential to enhance the usability of LLMs in tasks requiring precise structured outputs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.03305v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate executable outputs, JSON objects, and API calls, where a single syntax error can make the output unusable. Constrained decoding enforces validity token-by-token via masking and renormalization, but it can distort generation when the model assigns low probability mass to valid continuations, pushing decoding toward locally valid yet semantically incorrect trajectories. We propose \emph{Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding (DCCD)}, a simple two-step, training-free inference procedure that decouples semantic planning from structural enforcement: an unconstrained draft is generated first, and constrained decoding is then applied, conditioned on this draft, to guarantee validity. We analyze DCCD through a KL-projection view, showing that draft conditioning increases feasible mass and reduces the cumulative "projection tax" induced by hard constraints, with an optional best-of-$K$ draft selection. Across structured reasoning benchmarks, DCCD improves strict structured accuracy by up to +24 percentage points over standard constrained decoding (e.g., 15.2\% to 39.0\% on GSM8K with a 1B model), and enables smaller model pairs to match or exceed much larger constrained baselines, yielding substantial gains in parameter efficiency.

items.title: Researchers localize and analyze policy routing circuits in alignment-trained language models from 2B to 72B parameters, revealing gating mechanisms that control refusal and safety behaviors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: How Alignment Routes: Localizing, Scaling, and Controlling Policy Circuits in Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have identified and analyzed the policy routing mechanism in alignment-trained language models ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters. They found that an intermediate-layer attention gate detects content and activates deeper amplifier heads that influence the model's refusal behavior. This gating mechanism, though contributing less than 1% of output, is causally necessary and consistent across multiple models from different labs. The study shows that modulating this gate can control the model's policy responses, from refusal to factual answering, and that safety behaviors are governed by routing rather than removal of capabilities.

The research reveals that in smaller models, the gate and amplifier are single attention heads, while in larger models they form bands across layers. The gating circuit varies by topic, language, and model generation, and operates early in the processing pipeline. Techniques such as interchange testing and cipher contrast analysis were used to map and verify the routing circuits. The findings suggest that any encoding that bypasses detection-layer pattern matching can circumvent the policy controls, regardless of deeper layer processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.04385v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We localize the policy routing mechanism in alignment-trained language models. An intermediate-layer attention gate reads detected content and triggers deeper amplifier heads that boost the signal toward refusal. In smaller models the gate and amplifier are single heads; at larger scale they become bands of heads across adjacent layers. The gate contributes under 1% of output DLA, yet interchange testing (p < 0.001) and knockout cascade confirm it is causally necessary. Interchange screening at n >= 120 detects the same motif in twelve models from six labs (2B to 72B), though specific heads differ by lab. Per-head ablation weakens up to 58x at 72B and misses gates that interchange identifies; at scale, interchange is the only reliable audit. Modulating the detection-layer signal continuously controls policy from hard refusal through evasion to factual answering. On safety prompts the same intervention turns refusal into harmful guidance, showing that the safety-trained capability is gated by routing, not removed. Thresholds vary by topic and by input language, and the circuit relocates across generations within a family even while behavioral benchmarks register no change. Routing is early-commitment: the gate fires at its own layer before deeper layers finish processing the input. An in-context substitution cipher collapses gate interchange necessity by 70 to 99% across three models, and the model switches to puzzle-solving rather than refusal. Injecting the plaintext gate activation into the cipher forward pass restores 48% of refusals in Phi-4-mini, localizing the bypass to the routing interface. A second method, cipher contrast analysis, uses plain/cipher DLA differences to map the full cipher-sensitive routing circuit in O(3n) forward passes. Any encoding that defeats detection-layer pattern matching bypasses the policy regardless of whether deeper layers reconstruct the content.

items.title: Researchers propose Evidence Graph Consistency framework for hallucination detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, revealing model-dependent patterns across six large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evidence Graph Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Model-Dependent Analysis of Hallucination Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Evidence Graph Consistency (EGC) framework to improve hallucination detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems used by large language models. Unlike existing methods that assess flat similarity between generated answers and retrieved passages, EGC constructs local evidence graphs for each response and calculates structural consistency measures to identify hallucinations. Testing across six large language models with 5,767 responses revealed distinct patterns: Llama-2 models showed expected diagnostic results, while GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and Mistral-7B exhibited reversed patterns, indicating different hallucination behaviors among model families.

This study highlights that embedding-based graph consistency measures cannot universally detect hallucinations across all model types, suggesting the need for model-specific approaches. The findings provide new insights into the structural relationships between evidence and generated claims, advancing understanding of hallucination phenomena in language models and guiding future development of more reliable detection techniques.

items.originalTitle: Quantifying Subliminal Behavioral Transfer Ratios in Language Model Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers have quantified the subliminal transfer of undesirable behaviors during language model distillation, a process where a student model learns from a teacher model. Using two teacher models, Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, they varied steering strengths and distilled student models with only benign data. Evaluation on 100 JailbreakBench prompts by GPT-4.1 revealed that subliminal behavioral transfer is robust but differs in scaling between models, with Llama-2 showing a sharp threshold and Qwen2.5 exhibiting continuous and higher transfer levels.

This study systematically measures the magnitude of subliminal learning, which occurs when unwanted traits from the teacher model inadvertently pass to the student model despite efforts to transfer only benign behavior. The findings highlight distinct transfer dynamics for the two models, providing insight into how steering strength influences the degree of behavioral transfer during distillation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.11270v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distillation of a language model intended to transfer benign behavior to a student model may also transfer undesirable characteristics, if they are present in the teacher model, a phenomenon known as subliminal learning. This study quantifies subliminal behavioral transfer ratios by steering two teacher models (Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) at varying steering strengths and distilling student models using only benign data. Evaluation on 100 JailbreakBench prompts with GPT-4.1, serving as the evaluator, indicates that transfer is robust but exhibits distinct scaling behaviors. items.title: Researchers find lossy memory in language models leads to worse performance than empty memory, proposing a source-first policy to restore correctability across eight models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reclaim Evaluation: A Lossy Memory Is Worse Than an Empty One
items.summary:
Researchers have found that lossy memory in language models can lead to worse performance than having no memory at all. When a model retains incorrect conclusions but loses the underlying reasoning, it confidently produces stale answers, whereas an empty memory would cause it to abstain. This phenomenon, termed brittle memory, was evaluated across eight models using a method called reclaim evaluation, which compresses interactions and tests if corrections can recover the correct answers. The study revealed that lossy memory never outperforms empty memory and is particularly detrimental for models inclined to answer rather than abstain.

To address this, the researchers propose a simple source-first policy that preserves the original source information while discarding the derived conclusions. This approach restores the model's ability to correct errors within the same memory budget and was effective across multiple models and real dialogue systems. The study also identified limits where this fix fails unless completeness is explicitly recorded. The research provides a controlled, judge-free evaluation framework and releases tools to support further investigation into memory mechanisms in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25449v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A language model's memory can be worse than no memory at all. A memory that keeps a wrong conclusion but drops the work behind it makes the model emit the stale value as a confident answer, where an empty memory would make it abstain; we call this brittle memory. We measure it with reclaim evaluation: compress a drifted interaction at a fixed budget, then test whether a correction recovers the known answer, scored against ground truth with no judge. Correctability is bottlenecked not by capability but by whether the answer-determining source survives compression, so an 8B model and a frontier one wall in the same place. Across eight models a lossy memory is never better than an empty one, and strictly worse on those disposed to answer rather than abstain. A one-line source-first policy, keep the recomputable source and drop the re-derivable conclusion, restores correctability at equal budget where the answer-determining source is compact and identifiable; a length-matched control rules out added text, and a deployable one-prompt form reclaims 0.49-0.88, rising toward the oracle's 1.00 when a frontier model writes the note. The failure compounds through a memory loop and replicates on three deployed memory systems and on real dialogue (MultiWOZ), with a located boundary past which the fix fails silently unless the note records its completeness. This is a controlled study of a mechanism: judge-free exact scoring, matched-budget controls, and validators built to come out false; we release the harness, the paired memory conditions, and these validators.

items.originalTitle: CARVE: Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency for Chunk-Parallel Linear Attention
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CARVE (Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency), a novel recurrent model that improves linear attention efficiency and performance on reasoning benchmarks while using less memory and fewer parameters. CARVE addresses key limitations in previous architectures by implementing a content-aware erase mechanism that operates only on the key axis, enabling more effective memory management and maintaining compatibility with efficient training solvers.

The model reuses existing recurrent output tensors as signals for its erase gate and simplifies gating projections, resulting in better performance without increasing computational overhead. Tested with 1.3 billion parameters on 100 billion tokens, CARVE outperforms previous recurrent baselines on multiple common-sense reasoning tasks and sets new state-of-the-art results on retrieval benchmarks, all while reducing peak memory usage by 13% and parameter count by 19%. The approach is supported by formal theoretical proofs covering aspects such as memory capacity and stability.
